subject: Post Class Notes and Invitation to Connect
---

Hi {{var:first_name}},

Thank you for the time and openness that you offered in the CSPO training. What a fun bunch you were to work with. It's impossible to fit everything into just a few days so I hope this is just the beginning of our exploration of Scrum together, and that from here you'll take what you learned and expand that in your own environment.

You've just finished an intensive training workshop and your head might be buzzing with ideas and questions. That's great, but we don't want you to have to "drink from the firehose" any more. We've packed this email with resources to support you, step by step, on your path to success.

You already know that I believe in going well above and beyond just providing the information needed for certification and that Scrum and Agile training can be fun and engaging, and not death by PowerPoint. I have two small asks:

**Leave a Google Review** — Would you please give five minutes of your time right now to leave a short review? It could help others feel confident about making the same training choice that you did: [https://g.page/r/CXYNa8jWDGkuEAI/review](https://g.page/r/CXYNa8jWDGkuEAI/review)

**Connect on LinkedIn** — Send me a connect invitation at [linkedin.com/in/marklevison](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marklevison). If you post about your experience or what you learned, tag me or mention [Agile Pain Relief](https://www.linkedin.com/company/agile-pain-relief-consulting/) — I'd love to celebrate your achievement and share it with our community.

Thank you. It helps heaps.

Cheers,

~ Mark

---

**PLEASE KEEP THIS EMAIL** in a safe place somewhere. It's long, because we've crammed a bunch of helpful resources into it for you, but each item is designed to give you the most bang for your buck as well as for your time and efforts toward learning.

## Workshop Materials

Copies of your specific workshop murals can be found in this Dropbox folder:

**[Course Training Materials]({{var:training_folder}})**

In the spirit of kaizen, course material is always evolving and improving (with the help of your feedback, hint, hint). Long after you leave the workshop, you can download the newest and best version of the Certified Scrum Product Owner workbook again for free:

**[Certified Scrum Product Owner Workbook]({{var:workbook_link}})**

Here are links specifically for topics that we discussed in class:

**GenAI and the Future of Product Work**

- [How GenAI Actually Works](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/human-powered-ai-a-fun-way-to-understand-how-gen-ai-really-works/)
- [The Human Cost of GenAI](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/the-human-cost-of-genai/)
- [GenAI and the Feature Factory](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/gen-ai-and-the-feature-factory-automating-away-collaboration/)

You will also find all of these and more in our [World's Largest Opinionated Agile Reference Library and Glossary](https://agilepainrelief.com/glossary/). It's a cheeky title, but I strongly encourage you to check it out and click around. It has books I mentioned in class, along with different sites and resources, all in one handy place by topic. It will be a key resource to helping you solve whatever pain point you have.

And if you're looking for something that you can't find there, tell me. As you may have deduced in the workshop, I'm happy for any excuse to buy a new book or hunt for new resources.

Recommended books for Product Owners:

[https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/recommended-books-for-product-owners/](https://agilepainrelief.com/blog/recommended-books-for-product-owners/)

## Subscribe to our Alumni Newsletter

It's the primary route for us to provide ongoing support and additional resources to you.

PLUS: you'll get a free copy of Mark's eBook, The Guide to Effective Agile Retrospectives and the support series of emails with practical tips.

After subscribing you'll get an email asking you to confirm. Just respond as directed. You can unsubscribe at any time, but hopefully you'd tell us why so we can improve.

[Subscribe](CAKEMAIL_NEWSLETTER_SIGNUP_URL)

If the link doesn't work, try copying & pasting this url:
CAKEMAIL_NEWSLETTER_SIGNUP_URL

Keep in touch! We genuinely want to hear about your challenges and achievements. If you're on LinkedIn, send a CONNECT invitation at [http://www.linkedin.com/in/marklevison](http://www.linkedin.com/in/marklevison).

Cheers,

Mark (and the APR Team)

## Agile Networking

We have a section in our Newsletter called "Agile Networking" - a virtual bulletin board kind of thing. It's where prospective employees and employers can share a brief paragraph about themselves to help network and possibly reach receptive eyes. It's also where we share information about upcoming Agile/Scrum community events (meet-ups, workshops, etc).

So if you are looking for a job or to hire and would like us to include your information in our next newsletter, email us at contact@agilepainrelief.com. Also, if you know of an upcoming Agile/Scrum event in your community, please let us know so we can help spread the word on those too.

## Pay It Forward

Many who attend our public courses go on to tell colleagues and friends about them, and it's how a large portion of our workshops are booked. Mark is honoured and grateful when you recommend his teaching to others, so we're sharing that warm and fuzzy feeling and making it even easier to Pay it Forward. Now when you tell someone who could benefit from Scrum training and certification about Agile Pain Relief courses, you can give them the code: **PAYITFORWARD**. They'll get $150 savings on the regular price of any of our courses, and you'll get all the credit for telling them about it, with our thanks!

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

- Prioriti… [truncated]

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Generate a batch of evergreen social media posts (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky) promoting the AI Failure Modes quiz and existing blog posts / glossary entries. Use when Mark says "create posts", "schedule social media", "draft an evergreen batch", or asks for N days of social content. Outputs a single JSON file the posting pipeline can consume, and marks the source calendars so the same content isn't promoted twice.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (Mastodon 500 chars, Bluesky 290 chars).
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

import HighlightBox from '@/components/global/highlight-box.astro';
import LinkList from '@/components/global/link-list.astro';

**Release Frequency** is how often working software reaches real users. Releasing more often is, in the long term, the cheaper and safer bet.

How often should you release? For a long time the answer was: only when we had a large batch of features to sell. In the 1990s, when our software was shipped on floppy disks or CD-ROMs, this made some sense.

In the traditional approach to software development, we did what we called big bang releases, where we waited until the end of the quarter or the end of the year to release our software. We would spend months working on features, doing light testing along the way, then cram much of the real testing and other efforts into the last few weeks. This led to a lot of stress and overtime. In addition, products always went out the door with a lot of bugs. The question was not how many bugs, but how severe they were.

Every release is a batch of changes. The bigger the batch, the worse each of these problems gets.

## Problems With Big Bang Releases

- Testing cost grows faster than the scope of the release, because we need to test not just the new features, but also their interactions.
- The more changes there are, the harder it is to find where the defects are so we can fix them.
- The longer it has been since we last worked on a piece of code, the harder it is to understand, and therefore fix, a defect.
- Less feedback from the customer on the features we build. No matter how much User Acceptance Testing we do, it's not until the customer starts using the product in anger that they tell us what is hard to use and what is missing.
- The customer only ever sees big batches, so they don't trust you to build a small version of a feature and make it better later. If they don't demand everything and the kitchen sink in the first release, they don't believe they will ever get it.
- Some of the features we build will be obsolete by the time we release. The world around us is changing at an ever faster rate, and the longer the release cycle, the more likely it is to contain features that are no longer relevant.

## But Users Don't Want Constant Changes?

The most common objection is that users don't want to deal with frequent changes. This misses a few key points:

- Not all changes need to be available all the time. Limited use of Feature Flags can delay access to a feature until the audience is ready.
- When we release frequently, most of the changes are small, so they're easier to absorb. Many are based on feedback from users, and so are welcomed.
- Most people are already used to frequent changes. We use smartphones and don't notice most of the updates to the apps we use daily.

## Release More Often, Not Less

Here's a rule of thumb the agile community has spent years learning: if something hurts or is hard to do, do it more often. If it's hard to release, then release more often.

With a Scrum Team that has a good Definition of Done, I would expect to increase the frequency of releases. If needed, go step by step: quarterly, to monthly, to every two weeks, and eventually just move to DevOps.
